doc.title: Tom Albert and Milton "Mooney" Martin Interview, 1964-12-21

chapter: Eddie Vinson and the Pacific Brass Band
title: The Pacific Brass Band: size, instruments, leader and Georgia Hooker
summary: Martin and Russell work out the Pacific band's instrumentation and that it dates back to the 1880s and the Spanish-American War, not to the railroad. Its leader was Joel Lizard, and they talk about the trumpeter Georgia Hooker.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: About how big a band was that altogether? About how many cornets did they use? Yeah, three cornets. Three cornets. Three cornets. How many trombones? Two. Two. And they used alto horns those days. Alto, alto, biotone, clarinet, bass, snare drum. Two drums, yeah. Yeah, two drums, yeah. Um, I remember Manuel Moneta told us something, I believe, about a band the Southern Pacific had, too. Did they have some of the fellows that worked for them? Well, they- Have a band for the Southern Pacific? I didn't know whether- Well, uh- That wasn't any connection then with the Pacific Grass Band or the Texas and Pacific Railroad. No. I thought maybe they named it after the fellows that worked at the railroad or something at first.

No. That band there, that band was up in the 80s. Pacific Band, cause them long, we were Spanish and American War. Yeah, that's right. Back there. Yeah, that's right. See, back there in 1895, all them people was playing-
They'd been playing that long, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Maybe longer than that. Who was the leader of the Pacific Band? At that, at the time I know- Joel Lizard. Joel Lizard. Joel Lizard. Yeah, Joel Lizard.
Joel Lizard. No, no, no, Joel Lizard.
Joel Lizard. Joel Lizard. Was the leader. But now, he was playing in there, in tough trumpet player, all of them.
I believe somebody said he played the little E flat horn.
Did he know that little E flat?
Yeah, tough trumpet. Yeah, yeah.
Joel, uh, now, Georgia Hooker, it's another man.
Yeah, I've heard of him, yeah. Tough on the trumpet.
See, tough trumpet players.
Harrison Barnes told us about, uh, Mr. Hooker, he'd worked with him when he came to town.
Yeah, well, now, when he come to town, he was a trumpet player. Yeah.
He got off that trombone, got on trombone.
Yeah.
And baritone horn, too, I guess he played.
Yeah, he played, well, pretty much all of them. He used to play biotone, too. He could play biotone. You did, too, Tom.
Yeah, yeah. And the alto.
Yeah.
Yeah, once you learned the fingering, you could play it. Yeah, yeah.
